If the glyph is too degraded to\n support any single class more than another, abstain rather than guess.\n \n+## Global boundary protocol\n+Use topology first, then geometry. Small, faint, slanted, or slightly curved\n+terminal strokes still count when they are visibly attached to the glyph; do not\n+require ideal printed forms. Conversely, do not infer a defining feature that is\n+not visible merely because the rest of the digit resembles that class.\n+\n+Key boundary checks:\n+- **2 vs 7:** A visible bottom horizontal foot/base, even short or lightly\n+  slanted, favors `2`. A `7` requires a true top bar joined to a long descending\n+  diagonal and must not have a bottom base. Do not label a glyph `7` from a\n+  diagonal stroke alone when the lower end turns into a base/foot.\n+- **3 vs 5:** A `5` may have a rounded or worn top corner, but it still needs the\n+  top-bar/left-stem/lower-bowl organization. A `3` requires two rounded\n+  right-facing lobes with no distinct top bar plus left stem. Do not reject `5`\n+  solely because the top bar is imperfect or because the lower bowl resembles\n+  the lower lobe of a `3`.\n+- **8 vs 9:** Count enclosed regions before interpreting tails. Two stacked\n+  enclosed regions separated by a central pinch/crossing is `8`, even if one\n+  side extends downward and resembles a tail. A `9` has exactly one upper loop;\n+  its descending tail does not close a second lower hole.\n+\n ## Label hierarchy\n - `digit`\n   - [[MD.digit.0|0 \u2014 single closed loop]]\n"
